items.definition: How strongly and how fast a person reacts to pressure; a tempo, not a character.
items.example: Her stress reactivity is high in meetings and low in front of a machine.

items.definition: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.
items.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.

items.definition: The feeling part of empathy: catching what the other person feels.
items.example: Affective empathy made her notice that the new engineer was frightened in the group.

items.definition: The thinking part of empathy: seeing the situation from the other person's side.
items.example: Cognitive empathy is what lets you guess that the deadline was the real problem.

items.definition: Stating your need, your limit or your disagreement without wrapping it in blame.
items.example: Assertiveness is saying the report is late and then saying what you need instead.

items.definition: The leaning that keeps the peace by not raising the issue at all.
items.example: Conflict avoidance kept the meeting pleasant and the problem on the table.

items.definition: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.
items.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.

items.definition: The part of the value ranges of two groups that lies on top of each other.
items.example: The overlap between the two groups is wide, so the average says very little about one person.

items.definition: A rule about what a category of people is expected to do.
items.example: The gender role said the man pays, and the rule was never written down.

items.definition: The sense a person has of their own gender.
items.example: Her gender identity was hers to say, and nobody in the room had a vote on it.

items.definition: How a person presents their gender through clothes, voice, gesture and behaviour.
items.example: His gender expression changed when he started a new job, and the fit got easier.

items.definition: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.
items.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.

items.definition: A rule about what people should do.
items.example: It is a prescriptive norm: the expectation, not a description of what happens.

items.definition: What the people around you actually do, whether or not it is written down.
items.example: The descriptive norm here is that the whole team stays for the handover, and the expectation follows the team.

items.definition: The pattern in which one form of manliness becomes the standard everybody is measured against.
items.example: Hegemonic masculinity sets the picture of the man who never complains, and the man who does is treated as a smaller version of it.

items.definition: A situation in which a person is given two rules that cannot both be satisfied.
items.example: A double bind: be the one who decides, and be the one who notices that everybody is exhausted.

items.definition: The work of keeping other people fed, rested, healthy and connected.
items.example: Care work is the appointments, the meals and the phone calls, and it is still work.

items.definition: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.
items.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.

items.definition: The member of a couple who is expected to be the main earner.
items.example: As the breadwinner he carried the risk, and the risk became the whole family's.

items.definition: The work of running the house: cleaning, shopping, cooking, laundry and bills.
items.example: Household labour is the part of the week that never appears on a report.

items.definition: The strain that appears when one person is expected to be two things at once and the two pull in different directions.
items.example: The role conflict was not a failure of effort; two jobs had been given to one week.

items.definition: The talk in which two people change or confirm the roles they play together.
items.example: Role negotiation is not a quarrel about who is right; it is a decision about who does what.

items.definition: The gap between the number of relationships you want and the number you actually have. It is a feeling, and it can occur in a crowded room.
items.example: A full calendar and a lonely February are not contradictions.

items.definition: Being cut off from other people without choosing it, and without the comfort that solitude brings.
items.example: Working from home every day turned into isolation by February.

items.definition: The state of being estranged from the people around you, from a group, or from your own life.
items.example: He worked in the same team for years and felt alienated from it.

items.definition: Being alone by choice, with no element of loss or distress. It is not the same as loneliness.
items.example: Two hours of solitude on Sunday is what makes the week work.

items.definition: The practice of choosing fewer people and refusing more, so that the chosen ones get more of you.
items.example: Her selectivity is not rudeness; it is a policy she applies to everybody.

items.definition: A level of quality or a rule of conduct.
The belief that a partner must match a complete specification exactly, with no deviation allowed.
items.example: Hyperfidelity is why the search stops before it has really begun.

items.definition: A link between two facts, so that one explains, limits or changes the other.
items.example: There is a connection between the load on the pump and the life of the seal.

items.definition: The state in which both sides give and both receive, checked by asking each side what the other gives.
items.example: There is no mutuality here: one of them does all the giving.

items.definition: A decision to keep something going at a cost to yourself, made again and again rather than once.
items.example: Commitment is not one decision; it is the tenth one as well as the first.

items.definition: The state of being able to make the decision of commitment now, with the time, the wish and a picture of the cost.
items.example: He has the wish and not the readiness, and he can tell the two apart.

items.definition: The willingness to be known by somebody new, which is wider than being selective or not.
items.example: Openness is not saying yes to everybody; it is letting one more person in.

items.definition: A strong dislike that turns a possible approach into an immediate withdrawal.
items.example: Her aversion to that kind of meeting turned into a refusal before she had read the message.

items.definition: The state in which the same goal pulls you towards it and away from it at the same time.
items.example: The approach-avoidance conflict is inside him, not in the other person.

items.definition: One only; not multiple.
items.example: A single file is a gallery of one.

items.definition: The situation of being without a romantic partner, seen as a general condition rather than one person's story.
items.example: Long-term singleness has its own vocabulary, and its own pressures.

items.definition: Describing a person who has no romantic partner, without saying whether that is a choice.
items.example: He said he was unpartnered, and he said it without any apology in his voice.

items.definition: The repeated sense that a status such as being single is a condition to be explained, corrected or ended.
items.example: The social pressure arrives in small questions, not in one cruel remark.
